Köln: Rüdiger Köppe, pp. 91-92.
catalog_locator: Downing 2004: 109-110, section 2.4 'Chadic': second and third paragraphs and example set (5) 'Kwami stress (Leger 1994, pp 91-92)' on p. 109; closing sentence 'Clearly more phonetic studies..' is the first sentence of p. 110 (underlining).
catalog_quote: Chadic languages are all tonal, and it remains controversial whether stress is also a feature of these languages. As Wolff (1993) points out, even though stress has been reported for Hausa, for example, this is likely due to the fact that the correlation between vowel-length and High tone on particular syllables often strikes European ears as stress on that syllable. ... However, Kwami, a Chadic language spoken in Nigeria, is described by Leger (1994) as having stress in words that lack vowel length and High tone. According to Leger, while syllables with a long vowel are always stressed and initial High toned syllables or closed syllables also attract stress (when there is no long vowel), stress is also heard on the final syllable of words lacking High tones or long vowels. These points are illustrated by the data below (accents indicate tones; the stressed syllable is underlined): (5) Kwami stress (Leger 1994, pp 91-92) háakù 'yawn (noun)' gàrìngáalè 'bicycle, wheel' kábá 'inside' kòmkáy 'pluck' kùrè 'fence' [underlining as read from: h_áa_kù, gàrìng_áa_lè, k_á_bá, k_òm_káy, kùr_è] ... [p. 110] Clearly more phonetic studies of the correlates of stress in Chadic languages are necessary to disentangle this controversy.
sweep_summary: Kwaami (kwaa1269) is not in the catalog. The only title-keyword item, Downing 2004 (ZASPiL 37), was already held by the project; its Kwami paragraph (p. 109) is relevant but second-hand, summarising Leger 1994: 91-92: long-vowel syllables always stressed, otherwise an initial H-toned or closed syllable, and final stress in words with neither H tone nor length (háakù, gàrìngáalè, kábá, kòmkáy, kùrè; underlining verified on the page scan). The primary source, Leger's 1994 Köppe grammar, exists only as a paid publisher PDF or Harvard offsite print (a scan can be requested through your own library) - no open copy on archive.org, Google Books (no pages) or HathiTrust; priority high. Glottolog 5.1 lists no other stress/accent title for Kwaami; Leger 2014 (Fading Delimitations, paid PDF) and the Kaye 1998 word review (DOI 10.1080/00437956.1998.11673880, tandfonline 403) remain unread.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone language (all Chadic languages tonal) with word stress reported in addition: a syllable with a long vowel takes the stress; if there is no long vowel, an initial syllable that is High-toned or closed takes it; words with no long vowel and no High tone are stressed on the final syllable. I.e. prominence is governed by weight (VV > initial CVC / initial H) with a final-syllable default.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Downing's summary; Downing adds (p.110) that phonetic study of stress correlates in Chadic is still needed, and (p.109) that reported Chadic 'stress' may be a European-ear artefact of H tone plus length (Wolff 1993 on Hausa).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (isolated nouns/verbs in the examples). Second-hand: Downing paraphrases Leger 1994: 91-92; the German original was not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Downing's report and Leger's grammar both concern Kwami [ksq], kwaa1269, of the Gongola basin (Nigeria). Not to be confused with StressTyp/ISO 'ktf' Kwami, a Bantu language of DR Congo, which is the only 'Kwami' row in the StressTyp2 dump.

sources.note: p.109 (sec. 2.4 Chadic): reports Leger (1994: 91-92) second-hand: Kwami has stress partly independent of tone; long-vowel syllables always stressed; failing a long vowel, an initial High-toned or closed syllable attracts stress; words with neither H tone nor long vowel are stressed on the final syllable. Five examples with stressed syllable underlined: h[áa]kù, gàrìn[gáa]lè, k[á]bá, k[ò]mkáy, kùr[è]. p.110: 'Clearly more phonetic studies of the correlates of stress in Chadic languages are necessary'.

sources.note: Short morphosyntax paper (middle verbs), not a tone description, but grammatical tone is its diagnostic: Kwami verb classes are distinguished by the tonal marking of the singular perfect ending ('.. tonalen Markierung der singularen Perfektendung. Schematisch laesst sich..'), and middle verbs, though intransitive, take the transitive tone pattern (Tonmuster) after loss of the ICP elements (earlier excerpt). Same analysis as Leger 1994 (two verb classes 'durch eine kontraer tonale Markierung an den Suffix-Morphemen des Perfekt Singular kenntlich gemacht').
